text:
U.S. and German officials are meeting in secret to talk about drug prices.

AI generated Text-to-speech

LONDON — The Trump administration is launching a full-scale charm offensive across Europe to persuade governments to follow Britain’s lead to pay more for medicines.

U.S. embassies across the continent are being mobilized to deliver a message to European capitals: American patients are paying too much for medicines — around three times more than Germany for new drugs — and Europe better chip in.

If not, the bloc risks losing out on pharmaceutical investment and access to new drugs, two industry figures with knowledge of negotiations told POLITICO.

“Our view is that Warren Stephens (the U.S. ambassador to the U.K.) has done a very good job, essentially performing his role of representing the Trump administration and its interests,” said one industry figure.

“We are requesting U.S. embassies really lean in … helping spell out, if you were to follow the path of the U.S.-U.K. agreement, this is what that could look like for you,” added the industry figure, who was one of eight people from the sector POLITICO spoke with for this piece, and granted anonymity given the sensitive nature of ongoing negotiations.

That deal protected British pharmaceutical companies from U.S. tariffs for three years and sees the U.K. increase drug spending over the next decade. In return, the U.K. has increased price limits for innovative medicines.

U.S. diplomats are now eyeing Germany as a next target.

Europe’s largest medicines market is undergoing a huge overhaul of laws in its health care system, including rules that govern drug pricing. The intention is to cut federal spending on medicines. The U.S. wants Germany to increase it.

Government representatives from Washington are now holding secret talks with Berlin on drug prices, according to three people familiar with the talks.

Health Minister Nina Warken and Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche have been engaged in strictly confidential discussions with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services for months, the people said.

On the agenda: investments worth billions, trade policy and fair pricing.

“We are a bit jealous of the U.K.-U.S. deal,” said Christian Hilmer, managing director of the prescription drug market at Pharma Deutschland. “In Germany, the pharmaceutical industry is struggling to launch new drugs to the market.”

America’s strategy hinges on cutting bilateral agreements country by country, exploiting Europe’s fragmented health care systems that leave drug pricing largely in national hands.

The U.S. embassy in Berlin is sending their commercial counsellor Nathan Seifert to the U.S. embassy in London over the summer for staffing cover. One industry figure said the posting is partly so the Berlin team can learn from their U.K. counterparts how to secure a pricing deal.

The U.S. embassy in London declined to comment for this story, but pointed to comments the ambassador made at the time of the deal.

Right before Britain struck its deal with Washington, Stephens warned that should Keir Starmer's government not agree to pay more for drugs, American pharmaceutical giants would close their U.K. operations.

In a statement for this story, White House spokesman Kush Desai said: “President Trump has been unequivocally clear: other wealthy nations need to step up and pay their fair share for lifesaving pharmaceutical innovation instead of relying on American patients singlehandedly bearing the load.”

Following Europe’s heyday as a life sciences superpower over 30 years ago, investment has steadily drained out of the bloc — with no sign of stopping.

In 1990, 49 percent of global private pharmaceutical research and development took place in Europe. By 2025, that number halved to 26 percent.

U.S. pharma Eli Lilly and three other major pharmaceutical companies halted planned investments in the U.K. in quick concession last year, when U.S. President Donald Trump demanded European countries pay more for medicines.

Now, companies are doing the same in Germany.

Eli Lilly and German pharma Boehringer Ingelheim announced last week they were reducing billions of euros of planned investments in Germany in response to the country’s cost-cutting plans.

Some of the stalled investment in Britain were resumed once a drug pricing deal was struck with the U.S.

Still, European governments are wary of following Britain’s lead.

Countries are already grappling with squeezed public finances and sluggish economic growth. Many are also skeptical that conceding to the pharmaceutical industry would end the pressure campaign — fearing it would just invite more demands later.

“Sometimes, pharma companies behave like an adolescent kid that keeps asking for more and more, no matter how much you give,” said Yannis Natsis, director of the European Social Insurance Platform (ESIP), which lobbies on behalf of 46 social security organizations across 19 EU member countries and Switzerland.

America also doesn’t have the same leverage in EU countries as it did with the U.K.

The Trump administration had threatened three-figure tariffs on pharmaceuticals, and double-digit tariffs on countries. The U.K. deal was secured amid that uncertainty with one of its biggest trading partners.

The deal secured duty-free trade in medicines for three years.  For EU countries, however, a 15 percent U.S. tariff has already been set.

“Trade policy is largely an EU competence, whereas health systems and pharmaceutical pricing remain predominantly national competences,” said Graham Cookson, CEO of the U.K.’s Office for Health Economics. “That means Germany cannot necessarily obtain the most obvious trade concessions bilaterally, even if it wanted to.”

One other key area for leverage, however, could be Donald Trump’s most-favored nation (MFN) drug pricing policy, that kicks in from January.

That will see America match the lowest drug price from a basket of wealthy countries, including Germany.

Pharmaceutical companies have threatened not to launch their products in those basket countries, arguing they would lose less in sales by launching at a higher price in America than a lower price in all countries.

Britain claims it has secured an opt-out from Trump’s forthcoming pricing rule.  But wording in the deal is ambiguous.

Without Britain’s opt-out, one U.K. pharma figure warned: “It will screw medicine launches in the U.K.,” because it would impact the price in the U.S. “And everyone is going to want to protect their price in the U.S. markets.”

But even industry isn’t so sure Britain secured that protection. “We actually are still trying to figure this out,” another figure said.

To many in Europe, Britain’s agreement with Washington looks less like a win and more like a cautionary tale.

America and industry have touted the U.K. deal, but that’s not the reception it got in London.

Former U.K. Health Secretary Wes Streeting — who was widely viewed by industry as “absent from the pitch” — angered the sector after publicly announcing he commissioned a review into whether the deal represented value for money.

“You had Wes talking about how important the sector is for growth in the economy and then acting like that, which totally undermines credibility and authority,” one U.K. pharma figure cited above said.

Some observed the U.K. deal happened largely thanks to a key figure in government backing industry’s corner — Science Minister Patrick Vallance, a GSK veteran who was their former president of R&D.

Campaigners were equally alarmed — particularly by the lack of long-term assessment of how much the agreement would cost taxpayers — and are trying to revoke the deal in court.

“The UK government struck a terrible deal,” said Diarmaid McDonald,  executive director of Just Treatment which campaigns for access to medicines. “Permanent weakening of drug price controls that were the envy of the world … In return they got the square root of bugger all — temporary tariff waivers on tariffs that don’t exist.”

The government estimated the agreement would cost roughly £2 billion in the short term, but no official assessment has calculated the uplift over the next decade.

Economist Diederik Stadig from Dutch bank ING Research estimates the changes could eventually add between £2 billion and £3.5 billion in costs per year by 2036.

Critics also question whether Britain secured much investment in return.

“We don’t think this will lead to more investment,” said ING’s Stadig. “Price is not a silver bullet. If the U.K. wants more biopharmaceutical innovation, it should try and invest in getting more clinical trials.”

Even after securing concessions, the pharmaceutical industry is pushing for more.

Though major British drugmaker AstraZeneca recommitted to a long-stalled investment, its CEO Pascal Soriot called it only a “very positive first step.”

For Europe, higher drug prices seem an industry pipedream.

“We are already paying too much for medicines in Europe,” said ESIP’s Natsis. “Right now, the budgets are under unprecedented pressure and therefore asking to simply give a blank cheque is not financially sustainable.”

Louise Westendarp and Dan Bloom contributed reporting.

Update: This story has been updated with a statement from White House spokesman Kush Desai.

Warren Stephens also warns UK social media ban is “a little draconian from a freedom of speech point of view.”

The former mayor’s intervention offers one of the most revealing insights yet into his thinking on trade.

The health department said disclosure would “prejudice ongoing policy development, international relations and commercial interests.”

Varun Chandra will stay on as No. 10’s top business adviser and U.S. envoy.
